name: Material Aging and Temporal Depth — How Buildings Carry Time in Their Surfaces and How Occupants Read It
short_description: Buildings exist in time; positive aging increases fractal richness (natural materials), negative aging degrades non-fractally (synthetic materials); shearing layers determine adaptive capacity
structural_pattern: Buildings exist in time. Their materials change — stone weathers, copper oxidizes, wood darkens, brick mellows, paint fades, concrete stains. Their spatial organizations adapt — rooms subdivided, doorways widened, extensions added. Their cultural contexts shift — warehouse becomes gallery, church becomes concert hall. These temporal processes leave perceptually available traces that occupants read, interpret, and respond to emotionally. THREE TIMESCALES OF ARCHITECTURAL AGING: MATERIAL AGING (years to centuries) — Brand's shearing layers: Site (permanent), Structure (30–300 years), Skin (20 years), Services (7–15 years), Space Plan (3–30 years), Stuff (daily). POSITIVE AGING: Natural materials develop increased surface complexity through weathering — stone grows lichen in fractal patterns, wood develops deeper grain, copper patinates — moving toward D ≈ 1.3 optimum. NEGATIVE AGING: Synthetic materials degrade non-fractally — plastic yellows uniformly, concrete stains, sealant cracks — producing visual disorder that signals neglect. SPATIAL ADAPTATION (decades to centuries): Spatial anomalies carry narrative information. CULTURAL LAYERING (generations to centuries): Multiple cultural epochs in the building's fabric.
higher_order_principle: Architecture as temporal process. A building is not a static object but a process unfolding across multiple timescales. Occupants perceive this temporal depth through material wear, spatial adaptation, and cultural layering. Buildings that age positively (natural materials, fractal weathering, adaptive capacity) accumulate perceptual richness over time, becoming more rewarding to experience. Buildings that age negatively (synthetic materials, non-fractal degradation, inflexible design) lose perceptual quality over time. The temporal trajectory is a design choice made at the moment of material and system selection.

material_aging.positive_aging: Natural materials develop fractal richness through weathering (stone lichen, wood grain, copper patina)
material_aging.negative_aging: Synthetic materials degrade non-fractally (plastic yellowing, concrete staining, sealant cracking)

spatial_adaptation.mechanism: Spatial anomalies (added walls, widened doorways) carry narrative information about changing use

cultural_layering.mechanism: Multiple cultural epochs visible in building fabric — engages knowledge-meaning system

fractal_aging_hypothesis.positive_trajectory: Natural weathering increases surface fractal dimension toward D ≈ 1.3 optimum
fractal_aging_hypothesis.negative_trajectory: Synthetic degradation produces non-fractal visual disorder

aging_trajectory.description: Fractal dimension evolution over time: D(t) = D_max - (D_max - D_0) × e^(-t/τ)

optimal_range.description: Perceptual optimum near D ≈ 1.3 (Taylor et al.)

aging_time_to_optimal.description: Years until material reaches D > 1.20 (entering optimal zone)

concrete.note: May not reach optimal without intervention

causal_links.evidence_base: Natural weathering processes (erosion, oxidation, biological growth, mineral leaching) tend to produce fractal surface patterns. Well-established in geomorphology and materials science (Mandelbrot, 1982). The specific claim that weathering moves surfaces toward D ≈ 1.3 perceptual optimum is a theoretical extension — plausible but not directly measured on architectural surfaces.
Taylor et al. (2011) demonstrate that fractal patterns near D ≈ 1.3 produce maximal processing fluency and positive affect. This is the T1 mechanism applied to aged surfaces.

Brand (1994) argues compellingly that layer independence enables adaptation. Buildings where services are embedded in structure cannot update services without disrupting structure. Widely accepted in architectural theory but empirical validation is limited to case-study evidence.

The emotional response to old buildings (reverence, rootedness, connection to continuity) is widely reported phenomenologically (Zumthor, 2006; Pallasmaa, 2005) and consistent with evolutionary attachment to stable environments (Appleton, 1975). Mechanism not empirically resolved — likely involves knowledge-meaning, processing fluency, and episodic association.

scope_conditions: Applies primarily to buildings old enough to show visible temporal change — typically 10+ years for material aging, 50+ for spatial adaptation, 100+ for cultural layering
New buildings can simulate temporal depth (artificial patina, reclaimed materials, historical references) but the perceptual signal is different from genuine aging
Cultural context strongly modulates response: cultures that value antiquity (Europe, Japan, much of Asia) respond more positively to temporal depth than cultures that value novelty
Material selection at design stage determines the aging trajectory for the building's lifetime
moderators: Material choice: natural materials (stone, wood, brick, copper, iron) tend toward positive aging; synthetic materials (plastic, composite, vinyl) tend toward negative aging
Maintenance regime: appropriate maintenance supports positive aging (cleaning stone, oiling wood); neglect accelerates negative aging regardless of material
Climate: harsh climates accelerate weathering; tropical climates produce rapid biological colonization; arid climates preserve but can produce destructive salt crystallization
Cultural valuation of age: wabi-sabi (Japan), patina appreciation (Europe), versus clean-and-new preference (some contemporary contexts)

interactions.nature: T1 provides the fractal fluency mechanism. TP3 extends T1 temporally: natural aging processes move material surfaces toward the fractal optimum over time.
MAT4 describes how natural materials engage multiple sensory channels simultaneously. TP3 adds the temporal dimension: these multi-channel properties change and typically enrich over time.

MAT5 describes culturally conditioned material-affect associations. TP3 adds that aging itself carries cultural associations — patina signifies continuity, wear signifies use, adaptation signifies care.
Spatial adaptations over decades create new thresholds and modify existing ones. The memorial structure of an adapted building differs from its original design.
